attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own essay, stated as fact.

semantics.note: Pulls out the factual part ('already happened'). The claim about what American labs fear is set aside, which is correct because benchmarks can't test it.

contract.note: Reading 'open source' as open weights, 'similar' as comparable index scores and 'cheaper' as per-token price is the ordinary market sense. It is neither stretched nor narrowed, and it is needed because the speaker named no measure.

evidence.note: USCC report dated before the post keeps a January 2026 Artificial Analysis snapshot: Kimi K2.5 and GPT-5.2 both score 47 on the index, at about a quarter of the blended price.
Moonshot's own paper (Feb 2026) says the K2.5 checkpoint was released openly. This is a company disclosure, used only to show the open release happened.
ARC Prize (Jan 2025): R1 was comparable only to low-compute o1, so parity depends on settings. This limits a claim of full parity but not the existence claim.

reviews.rationale: A dated, independent comparison from before publication shows an open-weight Chinese model (Kimi K2.5) matching GPT-5.2 on an aggregate index at about a quarter of the price. That meets the support condition. e3 shows parity depends on the task, but the claim is about existence, not parity everywhere.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words. The Doctorow paraphrase comes in a separate sentence.

semantics.note: The revision restores 'vast, vast majority' and the $20/$200 plan tiers. The proposition matches the statement.

contract.note: Weighting by compute and using the Q2 2026 window are reasonable plain readings. Not treating API list prices as actual cost is fair to both sides.

evidence.note: Reports SemiAnalysis findings that plans lose money above a low usage threshold, but says typical users stay below it. This leans against the claim in part, but gives no compute-weighted share or affordability data.
Survey measures paid conversion per user, not compute consumed, so it cannot settle the share claim.

reviews.rationale: The packet has no breakdown of compute use by free, subscription, API and enterprise tiers, no actual serving costs, and no affordability data. e1 suggests typical subscribers are not deeply subsidised, but heavy users could still use most of the compute. The evidence does not settle the claim.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his essay.

semantics.note: 'It'll become blatantly obvious' is a firm forecast. The antecedent (media and corporate hype subsiding) is fairly condensed into 'once the AI hype subsides'.

contract.note: Reading the antecedent as a sustained, broad retreat in promotion (not literal silence) is fair. 'Weak demand' has no threshold, and the contract flags this.

evidence.note: CARMA describes AI media narratives shifting in H1 2026 while AI still dominates headlines. It does not show the antecedent (a broad retreat in promotion) happened.

reviews.rationale: The forecast is conditional and has no deadline. Nothing in the packet shows the antecedent, a sustained retreat in AI hype, had happened by the evaluation date, and there is no later evidence on demand. Under the policy an unmet or unknown antecedent is not scored, so the forecast stays open.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his essay.

semantics.note: 'Newsflash!' is rhetorical framing, but the core is a factual claim about what AI GPUs are useful for. The normalisation keeps 'not much else'.

contract.note: Plain reading: few substantial uses beyond generative AI. That is the ordinary sense. Counting demonstrated scientific workloads, without requiring the best price-performance, fits the word 'useful'. The economic-reuse subtext in the context does not narrow the sentence itself.

evidence.note: Vendor benchmark (June 2026) shows molecular dynamics, up to about 1M atoms, running on B200, GH200 and H100. Exxact sells these systems, so it has an interest. Its note that these GPUs are poor value for MD partly reflects the speaker's economic point.
June 2026 preprint runs quantum circuit simulation and many-body dynamics on DGX H100 nodes, scaling across several nodes. Non-generative work; not peer-reviewed.
June 2026 preprint runs finite-element material mechanics on A100 and H100 with large speedups over CPU. Non-generative; not peer-reviewed.

reviews.rationale: Within the target quarter, three sources document working non-generative workloads on A100, H100 and B200 data-centre GPUs: molecular dynamics, quantum and many-body simulation, and finite-element mechanics. This meets the contradiction condition (substantial use across several fields). The price-performance caveat does not change that usefulness.
